# Build-integrity profile

<!-- Generated by `obaaf docs build` from src/obaaf/data/. Do not edit by hand. -->

*Version 0.1, in active adoption with pilot teams. It may change in version 0.2 based on pilot feedback; open design decisions are tracked in [DECISIONS.md](../DECISIONS.md).*

Version 0.1.0 (released). Source: Paper 2, Table 4 (*Securing the Game Build*). The profile tailors NIST's Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) and SLSA to software build and release pipelines: 28 requirements in nine control families, each guarding one step on the path from commit to user. Developed with independent game studios and grounded in their pipelines, the control families apply to any team that builds and ships software; a few requirements name game-specific cases and are marked where they do not apply. Each requirement has a test that passes or fails, the evidence to inspect, and its mappings.

The requirement statements, the attack paths and properties each addresses, and the SSDF and SLSA mappings are quoted from the paper's Table 4. The titles, rationales, tests and evidence are new drafts written for this repository; they await the author's review ([DECISIONS.md](../DECISIONS.md), D-004).

## Isolation tiers

| Tier | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| A | A fresh environment for every build, where the toolchain allows it. Can meet SLSA Build Level 3. |
| B | Persistent hosts dedicated to the release lane: they never build unreviewed changes, accept no interactive sessions, restrict egress, hold no standing secrets, and are reimaged from a versioned image on a schedule and after any suspected exposure. Reported as below SLSA Build Level 3. |

Isolation tiers A and B are separate from the four self-assessment tiers.

## Attack paths and game properties

| ID | Attack path |
| --- | --- |
| AP1 | Build environment: the attacker altered what the studio's own build produced. |
| AP2 | Signing material: the attacker stole certificates or keys and signed malware as the studio. |
| AP3 | Publishing or update channel: the attacker pushed a malicious update through an account, server, or store the players trusted. |
| AP4 | Third-party component: malicious code arrived inside an SDK or dependency the studio shipped. |

| ID | Property of game development |
| --- | --- |
| D1 | Assets dominate inputs, and some can execute code. |
| D2 | Engines, middleware, and platform SDKs arrive outside package registries. |
| D3 | One project fans out to platform-specific build hosts, some persistent. |
| D4 | Builds depend on shared, writable derived-data caches. |
| D5 | Platforms take over signing and distribution. |
| D6 | Updates are frequent and often urgent. |
| D7 | Most studios are small and rely on partners. |

## F1 Source and assets

### G1.1 Protect release branches and streams

**Requirement.** Protect release branches and streams: changes need review, and build scripts, CI configuration, and engine and plugin code are owner-protected paths.

**Addresses.** AP1

**Why.** Build scripts, CI configuration, and engine and plugin code change what ships as surely as game code does, so review that covers only game code leaves the build path open. Owner-protected paths give the review that G1.2 relies on a person who must approve.

**Test.** For every release branch or stream, confirm that (1) changes cannot land without an approving review, and (2) the paths holding build scripts, CI configuration, and engine and plugin code have named owners whose approval is required. Pass only if both hold for every release branch or stream.

**Evidence.** Branch or stream protection settings; the code-owner file or path protections.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.1: Protect All Forms of Code from Unauthorized Access and Tampering · SLSA or other (Table 4): Source L3 · SLSA v1.2 requirements: Source L3: continuous technical controls · Assessment items: 1.6, 4.1 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-REPO-001`

### G1.2 Treat the build definition as code

**Requirement.** Treat the build definition as code: build graphs and packaging and signing steps live in version control, changes need approval by someone other than the author, and build hosts take configuration only from version control.

**Addresses.** AP1; D3

**Why.** Persistent build hosts drift, and configuration edited on a host leaves no review trail. Keeping the build definition in version control, approved by a second person, makes every change to how releases are built visible and attributable.

**Test.** Confirm that (1) build graphs and packaging and signing steps are stored in version control, (2) a change to them cannot merge without approval from someone other than its author, and (3) build hosts read their build configuration only from version control. Sample the three most recent changes to these files and check each was approved by a non-author.

**Evidence.** Protection rules on build-definition paths; a sample of recent changes; host configuration.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.1: Protect All Forms of Code from Unauthorized Access and Tampering; PW.7: Review and/or Analyze Human-Readable Code to Identify Vulnerabilities and Verify Compliance with Security Requirements · SLSA or other (Table 4): Source L4, for the build definition · SLSA v1.2 requirements: Source L4: two-party review · Assessment items: 2.2 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-REPO-001`

### G1.3 Attribute every change

**Requirement.** Attribute every change: individual accounts for every person and partner, with no shared logins.

**Addresses.** AP1; D7

**Why.** Change history only identifies who changed what when every person, contractor, and partner has an individual account. Shared logins also make it impossible to revoke one person's access without disrupting everyone.

**Test.** List the accounts in version control and CI. Pass if every account maps to exactly one person or one automated service, and no account is shared.

**Evidence.** User list for version control and CI, with owners.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.1: Protect All Forms of Code from Unauthorized Access and Tampering · SLSA or other (Table 4): Source L2 · SLSA v1.2 requirements: Source L1–L2: version control and change history · Assessment items: 1.7

## F2 Intake of third-party code, SDKs, and assets

### G2.1 Keep a binary manifest

**Requirement.** Keep a binary manifest: record every vendored binary, SDK, engine build, and plugin with its source, version, and digest, and fail builds on unrecorded changes.

**Addresses.** AP4; D2

**Why.** Engines, SDKs, and plugins often arrive as files from vendor portals rather than through a package registry, so dependency tools cannot see them. A manifest with digests turns an unrecorded change into a failed build.

**Test.** Confirm that a manifest lists every vendored binary, SDK, engine build, and plugin with its source, version, and digest. On a scratch branch, change one byte of a covered file without updating the manifest. Pass if the build fails.

**Evidence.** The manifest file and the build step that checks it.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PW.4: Reuse Existing, Well-Secured Software When Feasible Instead of Duplicating Functionality; PS.3.2: Collect, safeguard, maintain, and share provenance data for all components of each release. (task, summarized) · SLSA or other (Table 4): S2C2F ingest and inventory · Assessment items: 1.8, 2.6 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-008` · Tools: `obaaf manifest create`, `obaaf manifest check`

### G2.2 Quarantine third-party assets and plugins

**Requirement.** Quarantine third-party assets and plugins: open them first in an isolated environment without credentials and with automatic script execution off, and review editor scripts before they enter the project.

**Addresses.** D1

**Why.** Game assets can execute code: engines run editor scripts when a project loads, 3D model files have carried scripts that run when the file is opened with automatic script execution enabled, and engine resource packs have carried executable scripts. Opening a new package first on a machine with nothing to steal, with automatic script execution off, contains that risk.

**Test.** Confirm that a written intake procedure requires new third-party assets and plugins to be opened first on an isolated machine or virtual machine with no credentials and with automatic script execution turned off, and that editor scripts are reviewed before entering the project. Pass if the procedure exists and the most recent intake followed it.

**Evidence.** The intake procedure and the settings of the quarantine machine.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PW.4: Reuse Existing, Well-Secured Software When Feasible Instead of Duplicating Functionality; PO.5: Implement and Maintain Secure Environments for Software Development · Assessment items: 2.5

### G2.3 Review player-facing SDKs

**Requirement.** Review each player-facing SDK for data access and network behavior before adoption and on each update.

**Addresses.** AP4; D2

**Why.** Third-party SDKs run inside the game on every player's device. A marketing SDK with spyware features shipped inside 101 Android apps with more than 421 million downloads.

**Test.** For each player-facing SDK in the current build, find a review record covering the data it collects and the network destinations it contacts. Pass if every SDK has a record for its current version, dated before that version first entered a release build.

**Evidence.** Review records for current SDK versions.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PW.4: Reuse Existing, Well-Secured Software When Feasible Instead of Duplicating Functionality · Assessment items: 2.11

## F3 Build execution

### G3.1 Separate the release lane

**Requirement.** Separate the release lane: release builds run only on hosts that never build unreviewed changes and accept no interactive sessions.

**Addresses.** AP1; D3

**Why.** A host that builds unreviewed changes can be made to run attacker code, which can then tamper with later builds on that host. Persistent runners that ran pull-request workflows exposed release credentials in the PyTorch case, and attackers inside build environments shipped signed malware in the 3CX case.

**Test.** Confirm from the build-system configuration that the hosts or runner pools used for release builds accept no jobs triggered by pull requests, forks, partners, or agents, and that interactive logins to them are disabled. Pass if both hold.

**Evidence.** Build-agent pool configuration and access settings.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PO.5: Implement and Maintain Secure Environments for Software Development · SLSA or other (Table 4): Build L3, isolation · SLSA v1.2 requirements: Build L3: isolated, ephemeral builds · Assessment items: 1.4, 2.1 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-013`, `OBAAF-GHA-015`, `OBAAF-GHA-002`, `OBAAF-GHA-010`, `OBAAF-GHA-019`

### G3.2 Use tiered isolation

**Requirement.** Use tiered isolation: Tier A, a fresh environment per build where toolchains allow; Tier B, persistent hosts dedicated to the release lane, reimaged from a versioned image on a schedule and after any suspected exposure, with their builds reported as below Build L3.

**Addresses.** AP1; D3

**Why.** SLSA Build Level 3 requires a fresh environment for every build, which some console and Apple builds cannot meet with a studio's infrastructure. Tier B closes the paths that compromised persistent hosts while keeping the SLSA claim truthful.

**Test.** For every release target, confirm that the build record states Tier A or Tier B. For Tier A, confirm each build starts from a fresh environment. For Tier B, confirm the hosts are dedicated to the release lane and that the reimage log shows a reimage within the scheduled interval. Pass if every target meets its tier.

**Evidence.** Build records naming the tier; build-agent configuration; the reimage log.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PO.5: Implement and Maintain Secure Environments for Software Development · SLSA or other (Table 4): Build L3, for Tier A · SLSA v1.2 requirements: Build L3: isolated, ephemeral builds · Assessment items: 3.3, 3.4 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-013` · Tools: `obaaf attest build-record --tier`

### G3.3 Restrict egress from release hosts

**Requirement.** Restrict egress from release hosts to package mirrors, platform upload endpoints, and the provenance service.

**Addresses.** AP1

**Why.** Unrestricted egress lets an implant fetch tools and send stolen data. An unexpected outbound connection is how the tj-actions compromise was first detected.

**Test.** Review the firewall or proxy rules for release hosts. From a release host, attempt a connection to a destination that is not on the list. Pass if the rules allow only package mirrors, platform upload endpoints, and the provenance service, and the test connection fails.

**Evidence.** Firewall or proxy rules; the result of the test connection.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PO.5: Implement and Maintain Secure Environments for Software Development · Assessment items: 3.5

### G3.4 Keep no standing secrets on build hosts

**Requirement.** Keep no standing secrets on build hosts: issue signing and upload credentials per job and short-lived, or use them through a signing service.

**Addresses.** AP2

**Why.** Credentials stored on a build host are stolen by whoever compromises it. Credentials issued per job and expiring with it limit what a compromise yields.

**Test.** Inspect build hosts and pipeline configuration. Pass if no signing keys, upload credentials, or long-lived tokens are stored on build hosts, and every such credential is issued per job and expires, or is used only through a signing service.

**Evidence.** Credential configuration; inspection of hosts for stored credentials.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PO.5: Implement and Maintain Secure Environments for Software Development · SLSA or other (Table 4): Build L3, unforgeable provenance · SLSA v1.2 requirements: Build L3: signing material inaccessible to build steps (unforgeable provenance) · Assessment items: 2.4 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-001`, `OBAAF-GHA-009`, `OBAAF-GHA-011`, `OBAAF-GHA-018`

## F4 Derived data and caches

### G4.1 Scope caches by lane

**Requirement.** Scope caches by lane: caches written by untrusted builds, workstations, or partners are never read by release builds.

**Addresses.** AP1; D4

**Why.** If release builds read a cache that others can write, anyone who can write to it can influence what ships. A poisoned CI cache reached the release build in the Ultralytics case, and an agent run steered by an issue title poisoned a cache used by release jobs in the Clinejection case.

**Test.** List every cache that release builds read, including engine derived-data caches, and the identities that can write to each. Pass if no untrusted build, workstation, or partner identity can write to any of them.

**Evidence.** Cache access permissions and the release build's cache configuration.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PO.5: Implement and Maintain Secure Environments for Software Development · SLSA or other (Table 4): Build L3, cache integrity · SLSA v1.2 requirements: Build L3: cache integrity · Assessment items: 2.7 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-006`, `OBAAF-GHA-007`

### G4.2 Regenerate or verify derived data for releases

**Requirement.** Regenerate or verify derived data for releases: release builds rebuild derived data or consume only content-addressed entries written by the release lane.

**Addresses.** AP1; D4

**Why.** Cooking can be intermittently nondeterministic, so cooked content cannot always be checked by rebuilding it. Treating cache entries as build inputs with an author lets the release lane trust only what it built itself.

**Test.** Inspect the release build configuration. Pass if release builds either regenerate derived data from scratch or read only content-addressed entries written by the release lane.

**Evidence.** Cache configuration for release builds.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.1: Protect All Forms of Code from Unauthorized Access and Tampering · SLSA or other (Table 4): Build L3, cache integrity · SLSA v1.2 requirements: Build L3: cache integrity · Assessment items: 4.4 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-006`

### G4.3 Check code artifacts by independent rebuild

**Requirement.** Check code artifacts by independent rebuild, recording expected differences and known engine nondeterminism.

**Addresses.** AP1; D4

**Why.** Build-time tampering leaves the source clean, as SUNSPOT showed by swapping a source file during compilation. An independent rebuild compared against the release exposes it, provided the rebuild host was not compromised as well.

**Test.** For the latest release, confirm that its executables were rebuilt on a separate host and compared with the released files. Pass if every difference appears in the recorded list of expected differences or known nondeterminism.

**Evidence.** Comparison report for the latest release.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.2: Provide a Mechanism for Verifying Software Release Integrity · SLSA or other (Table 4): Reproducible builds · Assessment items: 4.2

## F5 Signing

### G5.1 Hold keys in hardware or a key service

**Requirement.** Hold signing and upload keys in hardware, a cloud key service, or platform-managed signing, and log every use.

**Addresses.** AP2; D5

**Why.** Stolen code-signing certificates let attackers sign malware in a studio's name, as in the Winnti and APT41 campaigns. A key that cannot be exported cannot be copied by an intruder.

**Test.** Using the key inventory, confirm that every signing and upload key is held in a hardware device, a cloud key service, or platform-managed signing, and that the service logs each use. Pass if no key exists as an exportable file and the log shows the most recent use.

**Evidence.** Key inventory; key-service configuration; the usage log.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.2: Provide a Mechanism for Verifying Software Release Integrity · Assessment items: 1.5, 2.3 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-018`

### G5.2 Sign only artifacts with release-lane provenance

**Requirement.** Sign only artifacts that carry valid release-lane provenance.

**Addresses.** AP1, AP2

**Why.** A signing step that signs whatever it is given turns any build into a trusted one. Checking provenance first means only files the release lane built receive the studio's signature.

**Test.** Submit an artifact built outside the release lane to the signing step. Pass if the step refuses to sign it.

**Evidence.** The signing step's configuration and the refusal in its log.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.2: Provide a Mechanism for Verifying Software Release Integrity · SLSA or other (Table 4): Build L2–L3 · SLSA v1.2 requirements: Build L2: hosted build platform; signed provenance · Assessment items: 3.2 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-016` · Tools: `obaaf verify release`

### G5.3 Plan revocation and rotation

**Requirement.** Keep a written plan to revoke certificates and rotate upload credentials.

**Addresses.** AP2

**Why.** After a key is stolen, the time to revoke it decides how long malware signed in the studio's name stays trusted.

**Test.** Pass if a written plan names, for every signing certificate and upload credential, the owner, the steps to revoke or rotate it, and whom to notify.

**Evidence.** The plan, with named owners.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.2: Provide a Mechanism for Verifying Software Release Integrity · Assessment items: 1.5, 2.9

## F6 Distribution and updates

### G6.1 Upload from a dedicated identity

**Requirement.** Upload from a dedicated identity with only publishing permissions, as Steam recommends.

**Addresses.** AP3; D5

**Why.** An upload identity that holds only the permissions uploads need limits what a stolen pipeline credential can do: it cannot change who has access, or anything else that the other permissions cover. On Steam, the build account needs only Edit App Metadata and Publish App Changes To Steam, for the one app.

**Test.** Inspect the permissions of the identity used by automated uploads. Pass if it is used only for uploads and holds no permissions beyond publishing builds.

**Evidence.** The account's permissions in the store's partner portal.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PO.5: Implement and Maintain Secure Environments for Software Development · Assessment items: 1.2

### G6.2 A person sets builds live

**Requirement.** Require a person to set a build live on a public channel, and two people at the highest tier.

**Addresses.** AP3; D5

**Why.** Hijacked publishing accounts pushed malicious updates to released games in 2023. A person setting each build live keeps an automated path from reaching players unseen. It does not stop someone who has taken over that person's account; at the highest tier, a second person does (Paper 2, section 7.1).

**Test.** Inspect the release procedure and store settings. Pass if no automated step can set a build live on a public channel; at Tier 4, pass only if two different people must confirm on every path that can set a build live, including the store's own interface.

**Evidence.** Release procedure; store release settings; approval records.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.4 (draft 1.2): Ensure Software Updates Are Robust and Reliable · SLSA or other (Table 4): Analogous to Source L4 · Assessment items: 1.3, 4.3 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-014`

### G6.3 MFA and alerts on publishing accounts

**Requirement.** Protect every publishing account with multi-factor authentication, and alert on set-live events and permission changes.

**Addresses.** AP3

**Why.** Multi-factor authentication stops a stolen password alone. It does not stop a stolen session, as in the Downfall mod case; alerts on set-live events and permission changes report what such a session does, so the studio can react.

**Test.** Pass if every account that can publish builds requires multi-factor authentication, and a recent alert shows that set-live events and permission changes notify a named person.

**Evidence.** Security settings of each publishing account; alert configuration and a recent alert.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PO.5: Implement and Maintain Secure Environments for Software Development · Assessment items: 1.1, 2.12

### G6.4 Staged rollout with a tested rollback

**Requirement.** Roll out live updates in stages, with a tested rollback.

**Addresses.** D6

**Why.** Frequent, urgent updates leave little time for review. Staged rollout limits how many players a bad update reaches before it is noticed, and a tested rollback makes recovery fast.

**Test.** Pass if live updates are released to a fraction of players first, and a rollback has been tested within the last six months.

**Evidence.** Rollout configuration; record of a rollback test.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.4 (draft 1.2): Ensure Software Updates Are Robust and Reliable · Assessment items: 3.8

### G6.5 Updaters verify signatures

**Requirement.** Make self-hosted launchers and patchers verify update signatures with keys not stored on the update server.

**Addresses.** AP3

**Why.** The 2013 campaign delivered malware through an official update server. Updaters that verify signatures made with keys kept off the server survive a server compromise.

**Test.** Pass if the launcher or patcher rejects an update whose signature does not verify, and the signing key is not stored on any update server.

**Evidence.** Updater code or vendor documentation; key inventory.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.2: Provide a Mechanism for Verifying Software Release Integrity · SLSA or other (Table 4): The Update Framework · Assessment items: 2.10

## F7 Provenance

### G7.1 Emit signed provenance

**Requirement.** Emit signed provenance for every platform artifact, listing source revision, asset revision, manifest digest, SDK versions, and builder identity.

**Addresses.** AP1; D5

**Why.** Build-time tampering leaves the source clean, so detecting it needs evidence about the build itself. Signed provenance binds each artifact to the source, assets, manifest, SDKs, and builder that produced it.

**Test.** For every platform artifact of the latest release, verify its signed provenance. Pass if the signature verifies and the provenance names the source revision, asset revision, manifest digest, SDK versions, and builder identity.

**Evidence.** Provenance for the latest release.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.3.2: Collect, safeguard, maintain, and share provenance data for all components of each release. (task, summarized) · SLSA or other (Table 4): Build L1–L2 · SLSA v1.2 requirements: Build L1: provenance exists; Build L2: hosted build platform; signed provenance · Assessment items: 3.1 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-017` · Tools: `obaaf attest build-record`, `obaaf verify release`

### G7.2 Verify provenance before upload

**Requirement.** Verify provenance against policy, in a separate step, before any upload to a store.

**Addresses.** AP1, AP3; D5, D6

**Why.** When a platform re-signs or distributes a build, the moment before upload is the last point at which a studio can bind an artifact to its own pipeline. Provenance not checked there cannot be checked by anyone downstream.

**Test.** Confirm a separate pipeline step verifies provenance against policy before every upload. Run the release with an artifact that lacks provenance. Pass if the upload is blocked.

**Evidence.** The pipeline step and its log for the latest release.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.2: Provide a Mechanism for Verifying Software Release Integrity · SLSA or other (Table 4): Build-track verification · SLSA v1.2 requirements: Build track: verification of artifacts against provenance · Assessment items: 3.2 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-016` · Tools: `obaaf verify release`

### G7.3 Archive releases read-only

**Requirement.** Archive released artifacts, symbols, and provenance read-only.

**Addresses.** All

**Why.** A read-only archive lets the studio prove later what it shipped, compare it with a suspected tampered build, and investigate an incident.

**Test.** Pass if the artifacts, symbols, and provenance of the latest release are stored where no pipeline or user identity can change or delete them.

**Evidence.** Archive permissions or retention settings.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.3.1: Archive each release's files and supporting data, such as integrity verification information and provenance data. (task, summarized) · Assessment items: 3.9

## F8 Automation and AI agents

### G8.1 Bound agent authority by input trust

**Requirement.** Bound the authority of agents and bots by the trust of their inputs; agents triggered by player reports, community issues, or partner content run without secrets (companion R1–R4, R7).

**Addresses.** AP1, AP3

**Why.** An agent follows instructions found in the text it reads, and outsiders can write that text. An agent may therefore do no more than the least-trusted author of its inputs could do directly.

**Test.** For every agent or bot that player, community, or partner content can trigger, confirm that it runs with a read-only token, no secrets, no permission to request cloud credentials, and no write access to protected branches, and that a separate approved job applies its proposals. Pass if all hold.

**Evidence.** Workflow permissions for each agent.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PO.5: Implement and Maintain Secure Environments for Software Development · Agent controls: R1, R2, R3, R4, R7 · Assessment items: 3.6 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-001`, `OBAAF-GHA-003`, `OBAAF-GHA-004`, `OBAAF-GHA-005`, `OBAAF-GHA-010`, `OBAAF-GHA-011`, `OBAAF-GHA-020`, `OBAAF-GHA-022`

### G8.2 Protect agent instructions as code

**Requirement.** Protect agent instruction and workflow files as code (companion R5).

**Addresses.** AP1

**Why.** Poisoned instruction files persist across runs. Hidden characters in a rules file were the vector in the Rules File Backdoor case.

**Test.** Confirm that agent instruction files and the workflows that invoke agents require code-owner review, are scanned for hidden characters, and are loaded from the protected base branch rather than from the change under review. Pass if all three hold.

**Evidence.** Protection rules on those paths; the scan result; the agent workflow.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.1: Protect All Forms of Code from Unauthorized Access and Tampering · SLSA or other (Table 4): Source L3 · SLSA v1.2 requirements: Source L3: continuous technical controls · Agent controls: R5 · Assessment items: 3.7 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-REPO-001`, `OBAAF-REPO-002`, `OBAAF-INS-001`, `OBAAF-GHA-012`

### G8.3 Attest agent runs and verify them before release

**Requirement.** Attest agent runs, and verify agent-authored changes before release (companion R8).

**Addresses.** AP1

**Why.** A signed record of what each agent run saw, could do, and produced lets the release lane refuse changes that did not go through the approved agent path.

**Test.** Confirm that every agent run produces a signed agent-run record. Add an agent-authored commit without a record to a test release. Pass if the release verifier blocks it.

**Evidence.** Attestations for agent-authored commits in the latest release.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PS.3.2: Collect, safeguard, maintain, and share provenance data for all components of each release. (task, summarized) · SLSA or other (Table 4): Build provenance · SLSA v1.2 requirements: Build L1: provenance exists · Agent controls: R8 · Assessment items: 4.5 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-021` · Tools: `obaaf attest agent-run`, `obaaf attest approval`, `obaaf verify release`

## F9 Partners

### G9.1 Scope and expire partner access

**Requirement.** Give contractors and porting partners separate, scoped, time-limited access, and build their contributions in the untrusted lane.

**Addresses.** AP1; D7

**Why.** Console ports and outsourced work often go through third-party vendors. Scoped access that expires limits what a compromised partner account can reach, and building partner work in the untrusted lane keeps it away from release credentials until it is reviewed.

**Test.** Pass if every contractor and porting partner has individual accounts limited to what their work needs, each with an expiry date, and their contributions are built only in the untrusted lane until reviewed.

**Evidence.** Access lists with expiry dates; the pipeline lane used for partner contributions.

**Maps to.** SSDF: PO.2: Implement Roles and Responsibilities; PO.5: Implement and Maintain Secure Environments for Software Development · Assessment items: 1.7, 2.8 · Checker rules: `OBAAF-GHA-001`, `OBAAF-GHA-002`, `OBAAF-GHA-019`
